article.overview: A sample sealing system closes a sample container so that the material inside is kept separate from the outside environment. Its purpose is to limit sample loss, alteration and contamination between collection and analysis, and in return missions for the whole journey to Earth. In the sources reviewed the system is usually a mechanism that closes a lid, cap or plug on a container and maintains a tight seal, often with a verification step. Three examples are described, but they are not the same kind of system: (1) the Mars 2020 (Perseverance) sample tube seal, a titanium sample tube closed by a metal seal inside the rover's sample caching system, with sealing on Mars from September 2021; this is Mars hardware, not lunar hardware, and is included because it is the best-documented hermetic sample-tube seal in the public literature reviewed; (2) the Chang'e-5 surface sampling and packaging system, a PolyU-developed system that closes the sample container on the lunar surface after collection and flew in 2020; and (3) the Apollo Lunar Sample Return Container (ALSRC), a triple-sealed aluminium box that kept lunar samples under a vacuum-like environment during return, where the Smithsonian unit examined is a ground-training container similar to the containers that flew.
article.description: A sample sealing system is a subsystem of a sample-handling chain. It is normally downstream of collection (drilling, scooping or capturing material) and upstream of storage, transfer or return. Three elements are typically involved: a container (a tube, box, bag or capsule) that receives the sample; a closure (a cap, plug, lid or seal) placed on the container; and an activation or closing mechanism that makes the closure secure, which may be a ram, a ferrule, a sweeping action that clears the lid's path, or a vacuum process. In the Perseverance system the closure is a separate seal cup that is pressed onto the tube and then activated. In the Chang'e-5 system a funnel and sweeping motion prepare the container so that the lid can close. In the Apollo system closure was performed under vacuum and the box had three seals. There is no single standard design, and the three examples differ in mass, environment and purpose; their numbers should not be compared directly.
article.scientific_purpose_and_applications: Sample sealing supports several scientific goals. Preserving volatile and gas-bearing content: Perseverance sample tubes are designed to contain rocks, regolith and atmospheric gases and are hermetically sealed on the surface of Mars to minimise sample loss, alteration and contamination [3]. Limiting contamination: the Chang'e-5 system includes a funnel to protect the sample container from contamination during regolith deposition [5]; Apollo containers used seals and covers to limit exposure before closure [7]. Preserving sample context for later analysis: sealed containers keep samples in a documented state between collection and laboratory analysis, which matters for studies that depend on gases, volatiles or the state of the material when collected. Supporting return-chain integrity: a tight seal reduces the chance that handling, temperature changes or transport change the sample before curation on Earth [3]. Applications that depend on sealing include the study of trapped gases, organic and volatile content, and comparison of samples across missions. These applications are general motivations; the sources reviewed do not quantify the scientific benefit of any specific seal.
article.operating_principle: Perseverance (Mars 2020): after a tube is filled with rock core, a small robotic arm moves the tube to one of seven seal dispensers and presses its open end against a waiting seal. The seal is then extracted from the dispenser and moved to a separate station where seal and tube are pressed together [2]. The seal is a separate titanium seal cup with a gold coating, activated by an internal ferrule; at the sealing station the hermetic seal is created by placing the ferrule into the seal cup and inserting a ram that applies the required activation force [3][4]. The mission requirement is a maximum helium leak rate of 1.0 × 10⁻⁸ standard cubic centimetres per second (scc/s) at room temperature [3]. NASA reports that the gap between tube and seal is about 0.00008 inches (0.002 mm) [2]. Engineers use a visual check after sealing: the distance between two rings outside the seal and the serial numbers changes once the seal is fixed [1]. Chang'e-5: the PolyU system deploys a funnel to protect the container from contamination while regolith is deposited; a sweeping action brushes away excess material so the lid can close fully; the sealing device then closes the container, which a robotic arm picks up for transfer to the ascent vehicle [5]. A separate in-orbit transfer mechanism moved the sample container between vehicles; that mechanism is a related subsystem rather than the seal itself [9]. Apollo ALSRC: the Smithsonian record for the training unit describes a triple-sealed aluminium box that kept a lunar-like vacuum around the samples, closed under vacuum so that internal pressure would not exceed lunar ambient pressure; Teflon film and cloth covers protected the seals on the Moon and were removed just before closing [7]. A Smithsonian Apollo 12 record reports that numbered Teflon sample bags were sealed inside the box; that full record was not retrieved and this statement relies on a search-result excerpt [8].
article.scientific_importance: The main scientific importance of a sample sealing system is that it preserves samples in a state that can be studied later. Perseverance is among the best-documented sample-tube seals designed to meet a hermetic requirement: a leak-test study of six flight-like Mars 2020 sample tubes concluded that the seals are likely to be very leak-tight, with leak rates below 10⁻¹³ scc/s [3]. The study notes that leak rates below 10⁻¹⁰ scc/s are below the detection limit of commercially available helium leak detectors, so the lower value required a more sensitive method [3]. The Chang'e-5 and Apollo examples show how sealing has been used in lunar sample handling. The Apollo containers were designed to maintain a vacuum-like environment around samples for return to Earth [7]. The Chang'e-5 system shows the lunar-surface part of this chain, in which a sample container is sealed by an automated system before transfer [5]. Sealing also has a documentation value: in the Perseverance case a visual check and serial numbers on the seal make it possible to identify a sealed tube [1].

physical_specifications.note: There is no universal specification for a sample sealing system. The examples below describe specific systems and state whether they flew, were built or are design targets. Values are tied to the named system and source. Where a value is not publicly specified it is recorded as null or as not publicly specified. The examples use different technologies and units and should not be compared numerically.

examples.name: Mars 2020 (Perseverance) sample tube seal and sealing station
examples.type: Flown Mars sample-caching hardware (not a lunar instrument)
examples.status: Flown and operated on Mars. The first cored sample was sealed on 6 September 2021 (sol 194) [1]. The seal for the 14th sample did not release from its dispenser (see known_anomaly).
examples.seal_design: Separate titanium seal cup with a gold coating, activated by an internal ferrule [3].
examples.hermetic_requirement: Maximum helium leak rate of 1.0 × 10⁻⁸ scc/s at room temperature [3].
examples.measured_leak_performance: Laboratory study of six flight-like sample tubes reported room-temperature leak rates below 10⁻¹³ scc/s; one tube was measured at eight temperatures from −51 °C to +42 °C [3]. These are laboratory measurements on flight-like tubes, not measurements of tubes in service on Mars.
examples.station_components: Robotic arm; seven seal dispensers; a separate sealing station where ferrule and ram create the hermetic seal [2][3].
examples.visual_verification: Distance between two rings outside the seal and the serial numbers increases once sealed [1].
examples.known_anomaly: The seal for the 14th sample, called Mageik, did not release from its dispenser; NASA's page says it 'encountered too much resistance and did not come free' and presents Martian dust as a hypothesis, not a confirmed cause. The Bore Sweeping Tool was used to clean the tube's inner surface near the opening, and the force needed to insert the seal during later attempts was reduced. As of the article text (published 3 November 2022) the seal had not released; current status was not verified [2].

examples.name: Chang'e-5 surface sampling and packaging system
examples.status: Flown. The probe soft-landed on 1 December 2020, and the system completed automatic sampling and packaging on the lunar surface [5]. Sample return completion is reported only in a search-result abstract for a separate transfer mechanism [9].
examples.developer: The Hong Kong Polytechnic University (PolyU) [5]. Design paper listed as [6]; full text not reviewed.
examples.container_function: Used to seal and store the lunar samples for return [5].
examples.sealing_actions: Funnel deployment to protect the container from contamination during regolith deposition; a sweeping action to brush away excess material so the lid can close; a sealing device that closes the container for pickup [5].
examples.seal_leak_performance: Not publicly specified in the sources reviewed.

examples.name: Apollo Lunar Sample Return Container (ALSRC), ground-training unit
examples.type: Apollo lunar sample container; Smithsonian unit is a ground-training container similar to the flown containers
examples.status: The museum states that this unit is a ground-training container, similar to the containers that flew to the Moon, and that two ALSRCs were used on each mission [7].
examples.manufacturer: Union Carbide Nuclear Division, as listed by the Smithsonian [7].
examples.materials: 7075 AA aluminium case with a 2024 aluminium alloy mesh lining [7].
examples.mass_note: Listed as 14.8 lb (6.7 kg) for this training unit [7]. An Apollo 12 record reports about 6.8 kg when closed [8]; these may not be the same unit.
examples.seal_description: Aluminium box with a triple seal; closed under vacuum so that internal pressure would not exceed lunar ambient pressure. Teflon film and cloth covers protected the seals on the Moon and were removed just before closing [7].
examples.mesh_lining_function: Helps absorb shock during the Earth-return flight [7].
examples.sample_bags: Numbered Teflon sample bags sealed inside the box, per a Smithsonian Apollo 12 record known only from a search-result excerpt [8].

physical_specifications.dimensions_and_proportions: The three examples differ in scale and function: the Perseverance seal is a small titanium seal cup and tube interface with a tolerance of about 0.002 mm [2]; the Chang'e-5 system is a 1.5 kg mechanism with a 360 g container [5]; and the Apollo training container is a 20.3 × 48.3 × 29.8 cm aluminium box [7]. The dimensions of the Perseverance seal itself and of its sealing station are not publicly specified in the sources reviewed.
physical_specifications.mass_and_weight: Masses are not directly comparable because they describe different items. The Chang'e-5 sealing and packaging system is described as 1.5 kg, with a container of about 360 g [5]. The Apollo training container is listed at 6.7 kg [7]. The mass of the Perseverance seal and sealing station is not publicly specified in the sources reviewed.
physical_specifications.power_requirements: The Apollo container is a passive container; no power system is described in the record reviewed [7]. The Chang'e-5 system's power requirement is not publicly specified in the sources reviewed. The Perseverance sealing station's power requirement is not publicly specified; the sealing action is motor-driven, as described by secondary sources only.

article.environmental_and_operational_requiremen: Sealing systems operate in environments that vary with the mission. Temperature: the Perseverance leak study tested one tube from −51 °C to +42 °C and found that helium leak rates correlated with temperature [3]; the study notes that temperatures during storage on Mars and future transport to Earth could also affect leak rates [3]. Vacuum and pressure: the Apollo container was closed under vacuum so that internal pressure would not exceed lunar ambient pressure [7]. Contamination: the Perseverance sealing process must keep contamination out of the tube, and the Sample 14 investigation showed that Martian dust on the tube interior can affect seal insertion [2]; the Chang'e-5 funnel and sweeping action serve the same purpose during collection [5]. Mechanical loads: the Apollo container's mesh lining absorbs shock during return-flight loads [7]. Power: the Chang'e-5 system's power and thermal interfaces were not publicly specified in the sources reviewed.
article.limitations: The Perseverance sealing system is a Mars system; its performance in a lunar environment is not established. Leak measurements on Mars 2020 sample tubes are laboratory results on flight-like tubes and do not directly measure tubes in service on Mars. The Sample 14 anomaly shows that dust or debris can prevent a seal from being dispensed; the current status of this anomaly was not verified. Mass, power and envelope dimensions for the Chang'e-5 seal mechanism, and the seal technique used on its container, are not publicly specified in the sources reviewed. The Apollo figures come from a training unit, not a verified flight unit. Some Apollo sample-bag and handling statements rely on search-result excerpts from Smithsonian records that could not be retrieved directly [8].

transportation_and_deployment.overview: This is a sample-return payload. Its transportation role is to keep samples sealed through collection, transfer, return and curation. On Chang'e-5 the sealing device closed the container before a robotic arm picked it up for transfer to the ascent vehicle [5], and a separate in-orbit transfer mechanism moved the container between vehicles [9]. Apollo containers were closed under vacuum before return and were fitted with a mesh lining for shock absorption [7]. The Perseverance sample tubes are sealed on Mars [1][2]; the sources reviewed do not confirm the return schedule or return-chain interfaces for these tubes.
transportation_process: Containment and handling: the sealed container must survive launch, landing and transfer loads. Apollo containers used a mesh lining to absorb shock during return [7].
Sealing before transfer: on Chang'e-5 the sealing device closed the container before pickup by a robotic arm for transfer to the ascent vehicle [5].

In-orbit transfer: a separate pawl-linkage transfer mechanism moved the Chang'e-5 container between vehicles in orbit; this is a related subsystem, not the seal itself [9] (search-result abstract only).
Sealed sample return: Apollo containers were closed under vacuum before return, with seal covers removed just before closing [7]. The record does not state where every flown container was closed.
Earth-side handling: a search-result excerpt from a Smithsonian Apollo 12 record reports opening in a nitrogen-filled enclosure [8]; this was not verified against the full record.
Mars sample tubes: sealed on the surface of Mars [1][2]; return-chain interfaces and schedule were not verified and no transport or return conclusion is drawn.
transportation_and_deployment.deployment_methods: Not a deployable instrument in the usual sense. The sealing system operates as part of a sampling chain: a robotic arm presses the tube against a seal from a dispenser on Mars [2]; on Chang'e-5 a funnel, sweeping action and sealing device act on the container during surface sampling [5]; Apollo containers were closed under vacuum with seal covers removed just before closing [7], and astronaut placement of numbered sample bags is described only in a search-result excerpt [8].
transportation_and_deployment.historical_examples: Apollo lunar sample return containers (Apollo 11 to 17 missions, per the museum's statement that the unit is similar to flown containers) [7]; Chang'e-5 surface sampling and packaging system (2020) [5]; Perseverance sample caching and tube sealing (from September 2021) [1][2].
transportation_and_deployment.compatibility_assessment: No compatibility with any specific lander, rover or spacecraft is asserted. Compatibility would require verified interface data for mass, envelope, mounting, handling, thermal and power requirements, and return-chain interfaces. The Chang'e-5 transfer mechanism and sealing device are not transferable to another vehicle without verified interface data.

article.historical_significance: The Apollo ALSRC is a sealed lunar sample container designed for return to Earth, with a triple seal and vacuum closure [7]. The Chang'e-5 PolyU system is an example of an automated sampling and packaging system that seals a lunar sample container on the surface [5]. The Perseverance system provides a documented example of hermetic sealing for a Mars sample tube, with a first sealed sample in September 2021 [1]; its seal anomaly for sample 14 is a documented lesson about dust and seal insertion [2].
article.limitations_and_uncertainties: No single design exists; the three examples differ in technology, size, environment and purpose and should not be compared directly. Mass, dimensions and power of the Perseverance seal and sealing station, and of the Chang'e-5 sealing mechanism, are not publicly specified in the sources reviewed. Several sources were identified from search results or references and were not read in full: the Smithsonian Apollo 12 record [8], the Aerospace 2023 transfer paper [9], the Chang'e-5 design paper [6] and the Redmond et al. 2020 sealing-mechanism paper [4]. Claims relying on them are flagged. The statements that numbered Teflon bags were sealed in the box and that the box was opened in a nitrogen-filled enclosure rely on search excerpts from Smithsonian Apollo 12 records [8]. A Wikipedia summary of the ALSRC also reports knife-edge seals and high-temperature O-rings; this is not supported by the Smithsonian training-unit record [7] and was not treated as verified. The status of the Sample 14 seal after 2022 was not verified. Sealing systems from other missions (for example Luna, Hayabusa2 or OSIRIS-REx sample containers) were not researched in this pass. The current status of Perseverance sample return and any further Chang'e sample-return flights was not verified.

The Apollo ALSRC image_url is null because no direct asset URL was verified; the source page is retained.

data_quality_notes: Perseverance (Mars 2020) hardware is Mars hardware, not lunar hardware; included as the best-documented hermetic sample-tube seal reviewed. No lunar performance is implied.
Perseverance seal and sealing-station mass, dimensions, power and envelope are not publicly specified in the sources reviewed (null).
Perseverance Sample 14 seal status: the NASA article (published 2022-11-03) says the seal had not released; current status was not verified.
The NASA Sample 14 article names the sample 'Mageik'; a separate newer sample is named 'Amalik' in the same article. Only 'Mageik' is referred to in this payload.

Helium leak-rate values come from the Osterhout et al. 2024 Astrobiology study (PMC10795500), which describes six flight-like tubes measured in the laboratory. The study reports the mission requirement of 1.0 × 10⁻⁸ scc/s and measured leak rates below 10⁻¹³ scc/s; the study's detailed measured range was not fully captured, so only the stated bound is used.

Redmond et al. (2020), Journal of Spacecraft and Rockets, 57, 964-974, DOI 10.2514/1.A34681 was not read in full; publisher returned HTTP 403. Mechanism details are taken from NASA and the Astrobiology study that cite it.
Mars 2020 Sample Caching System paper (Space Science Reviews, s11214-020-00783-7) was not retrieved; the publisher redirected to a login page.

Chang'e-5 system: mass (1.5 kg system; 360 g container) is from a PolyU press release dated 2020-12-08; no peer-reviewed mass or dimension figures were verified. The Scientia Sinica Technologica paper (DOI 10.1360/sst-2021-0093) was resolved but its full text was not reviewed.

Chang'e-5 sample-return completion is reported only by a search-result abstract for a separate transfer mechanism (Aerospace 2023, MDPI 10(12), 992; publisher returned HTTP 403). Not verified against the full text.
No verified direct image URL was found for the Chang'e-5 sealing system; no image is included for that example.

Apollo ALSRC: the Smithsonian training-unit record (A20240027000) was read directly and supplies the materials, dimensions, mass and triple-seal description. The Apollo 12 record (A19772507000) was retrieved only as a search excerpt (direct retrieval returned HTTP 403). Statements on Teflon sample bags sealed inside the box and nitrogen-filled opening on Earth rely on that excerpt and are not verified.

The Wikipedia ALSRC article reports knife-edge seals and high-temperature O-rings and lists an en.wikipedia lead image with unclear licence. The article carries a maintenance banner about possible LLM-generated text. These claims were not treated as verified; the Smithsonian training-unit record does not mention knife-edge seals or O-rings.
Apollo Smithsonian record states the training unit is similar to the containers that flew; flight serial numbers and flight-unit specifications were not verified.

A secondary report (NASA-sourced coverage of Apollo 17 sample 73001, 2019) describes it as sealed in a vacuum container on the Moon and then in a second container; the NASA-hosted PDF could not be parsed and this statement is not included in the article.
The Smithsonian Apollo ALSRC image asset URL was not verified (HTTP 403 for Smithsonian object pages from this environment). image_url is null.
Sample sealing systems from other missions (for example Luna, Hayabusa2 or OSIRIS-REx) were not researched in this pass; the article is scoped to the three named examples.
Current status of Perseverance sample return and any further Chang'e sample-return flights was not verified as of 2026-11-13.
